title: Identical alpine species on distant mountains are relicts of the Glacial period

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Identical alpine species on distant mountains are relicts of the Glacial period

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: The same arctic and alpine species on widely separated mountain summits and in arctic regions are relicts of populations that spread across the intervening lowlands during the Glacial period and were stranded on mountains and in the far north as the climate warmed.

fields.label: Work
fields.value: On the Origin of Species by Means of Natural Selection, or the Preservation of Favoured Races in the Struggle for Life

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: Hence, when the warmth had fully returned, the same arctic species, which had lately lived in a body together on the lowlands of the Old and New Worlds, would be left isolated on distant mountain-summits (having been exterminated on all lesser heights) and in the arctic regions of both hemispheres.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci Origin of Species claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Charles Darwin, On the Origin of Species (1st ed., London: John Murray, 1859), Chapter XI, “Geographical Distribution”; section “Dispersal during the Glacial period co-extensive with the world”. Scope: arctic-alpine plants and animals of Europe and North America

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on darwin1859-ch11-11: resolvable-now, resolvability 0.81

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Multiple independent public data types record range shifts and population isolation. Species-specific resolution varies, but the historical mechanism is strongly testable for many focal taxa.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Combine dated pollen and fossil occurrences with population genomics and species distribution models to test lowland range continuity during glacial maxima and subsequent isolation on mountains and in the Arctic. Competing preglacial vicariance or independent colonization should predict different dates and routes.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Many species have idiosyncratic glacial refugia.

Pollen often resolves only to genus.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:
operationalizability: 0.89
data adequacy: 0.73
analysis feasibility: 0.72
data existence: 0.93
discriminating power: 0.73

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Glacial-age lowland fossils and modern ranges are in open databases and can test the geographic half of the relict hypothesis for many plants. Species-level identity of fossils and the genetic unity of summit populations are available only case by case. The full claim is decidable for well-studied European and North American taxa and not for the whole arctic-alpine biota.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: For arctic-alpine species shared among separated mountains and the Arctic, test whether last-glacial fossils occur in the intervening lowlands and whether genetic data show one recent northern population. Deep divergence among summit populations, together with no glacial-age lowland fossils, would count against a glacial-relict origin.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Survival on unglaciated peaks and later long-distance dispersal can mimic parts of the relict pattern.

Pollen and many macrofossils are not identified to species.

Range-wide genetic studies cover a subset of the European and North American biota.
